1. Abstract
This project builds a software system that estimates a person's eye refractive power (commonly called
"eye power" or spectacle prescription) without any specialized optometry hardware, using only a laptop
webcam and, optionally, a smartphone camera with flash. The core idea is optical: a nearsighted
(myopic) eye has a fixed maximum distance — the far point — beyond which it cannot focus clearly.
By using computer vision to measure how far a person is standing from the screen at the exact moment
a test symbol becomes unreadable, the system estimates the eye's power in diopters using a
well-established optical formula. A second, more advanced module uses the phone's camera flash to

well-established optical formula. A second, more advanced module uses the phone's camera flash to
analyze the reflex pattern inside the pupil (eccentric photorefraction) to classify the type and rough
severity of the refractive error. This approach is not a theoretical idea — clinically validated smartphone
apps built on the same principle have shown strong correlation with real optometrist measurements,
which makes this a credible, scoped, and achievable final-year project.
2. Problem Statement & Motivation
Access to basic eye check-ups is limited in many semi-urban and rural areas due to the cost and
availability of optometrists and autorefractor machines. Many people — especially students and

availability of optometrists and autorefractor machines. Many people — especially students and
children — go undiagnosed for years with mild-to-moderate refractive errors, which affects academic
performance and daily life. A low-cost, software-only screening tool that runs on devices people already
own (a laptop or a smartphone) can act as a first-level screening layer: it will not replace a clinical eye
exam, but it can flag people who likely need one, long before they would otherwise get checked.
Why this is solvable with software

Refractive error has a direct, known optical relationship with a measurable physical quantity:
distance.

Face and eye landmark detection is a solved, well-supported problem (MediaPipe, OpenCV) that
runs in real time on a normal laptop.

3. Project Objectives
1
Build a real-time webcam application that tracks the user's eyes and calculates live distance from
the screen.
2
Display a correctly-scaled visual acuity test (Tumbling E chart) that adjusts size as the user moves.
3
Detect the user's far point — the distance at which the test symbol becomes unreadable — and

3
Detect the user's far point — the distance at which the test symbol becomes unreadable — and
convert it into an estimated refractive power using the standard optics formula.
4
Build a secondary smartphone-based module that uses flash photography to classify myopia vs.
hyperopia and estimate rough severity using eccentric photorefraction.

5
Validate the system's output against the known glasses prescription of real test subjects and report
accuracy (average error in diopters, correlation).
6

4. Feasibility & Related Work
This project is feasible because near-identical systems already exist in published, peer-reviewed and
clinically tested form:
4.1 Smartphone far-point apps (Schepens Eye Research Institute, Harvard)
A smartphone app built on exactly this principle — measuring the distance at which small optotypes
(Tumbling E letters and grating patterns) become unreadable — was tested clinically across 201 eyes

(Tumbling E letters and grating patterns) become unreadable — was tested clinically across 201 eyes
with spherical equivalent power ranging from 0 to −10.2 D. App results correlated strongly with clinical
autorefractor measurements (Pearson R = 0.91), with average error of about 0.63 D for spherical power
and 0.28 D for astigmatism. This confirms the far-point method is accurate enough to be a legitimate
screening tool, not just a rough guess.
4.2 Eccentric photorefraction (GoCheckKids and academic research)
GoCheckKids is an FDA-cleared device (Class IIe) that uses a phone's ordinary camera and flash,
configured for eccentric photorefraction, validated against standard clinical cycloplegic refraction in

configured for eccentric photorefraction, validated against standard clinical cycloplegic refraction in
children. More recent academic work applies deep learning directly to these flash-reflex images to
estimate power automatically, confirming this is an active, credible research direction.
4.3 Key takeaway for scoping

Phase 1 (far-point method) is the well-validated, achievable core — build and test this first.

Phase 2 (photorefraction) is a strong stretch goal that differentiates the project, but should be
scoped honestly as classification (myopic / hyperopic / roughly normal + severity bucket) rather than
an exact diopter output.

Both phases require empirical calibration using real test subjects — this is standard practice even in
commercial tools, not a shortcut.



5. System Architecture Overview
The system is structured in five logical layers, moving from raw hardware capture up to the final report
shown to the user. Phase 1 and Phase 2 run as independent modules that feed into a shared
calibration and reporting engine, so either phase can be built, tested, and demonstrated on its own.

7. Phase 1 — Webcam Far-Point Method (Detailed Working)

7. Phase 1 — Webcam Far-Point Method (Detailed Working)
This is the primary, must-complete module. It works entirely on a laptop webcam and does not need
any special hardware.

Figure 7.1 — Step-by-step processing flow for the webcam far-point method.
7.1 Distance measurement — how it actually works
The system uses the Inter-Pupillary Distance (IPD) — the distance between the centers of the two
pupils — as its reference measurement. Average adult IPD is fairly consistent (roughly 54–68 mm),
which makes it usable as a scale reference once the camera is calibrated. The underlying relationship
is the standard pinhole camera model:
distance = (real IPD × focal length) / (IPD in pixels)
The focal length constant is calibrated once per camera: ask the user to sit at a known distance (e.g.,
50 cm, measured with a tape/ruler) and record the IPD in pixels at that distance. That single reference

50 cm, measured with a tape/ruler) and record the IPD in pixels at that distance. That single reference
point lets the system compute real-world distance continuously afterward, frame by frame, without
needing the user to do anything special.
7.2 The optotype (Tumbling E) test
A Tumbling E is a capital letter "E" rotated in one of four directions (up, down, left, right). It is preferred
over normal alphabet charts because it does not require literacy or letter recognition — the user only
has to identify which direction the "prongs" point, which keeps the test language-independent and
reduces guessing bias. The system displays the E at a size that is mathematically scaled to the user's
live distance from the screen, so that the visual angle it subtends stays equivalent to a real eye-chart

live distance from the screen, so that the visual angle it subtends stays equivalent to a real eye-chart
line at that distance.
7.3 Finding the far point
The user starts close to the screen (where the letter is easily readable) and slowly moves backward.
The system continuously re-scales the optotype to keep the effective test difficulty constant relative to
distance. The user presses a key or gives a voice response each time they correctly identify the
direction. The point where the user can no longer reliably identify the direction — confirmed with a
couple of repeat attempts to rule out random guessing — is recorded as the far point (F), in meters.

7.4 From far point to power
A myopic eye's far point is inversely related to its refractive power. Once F is known, the estimated
spherical power is computed directly:
Power (D) ≈ −1 / F (in meters)
Example: if a user's letters become unreadable beyond 25 cm (0.25 m), the estimated power is
approximately −1 / 0.25 = −4.00 D. The test should be repeated 3 times and averaged to reduce noise
from user reaction time and detection jitter.
7.5 Important constraint
This formula only works cleanly for myopia (nearsightedness), because a myopic eye has a genuine,
fixed far point. Hyperopia (farsightedness) does not have a comparable far point in the same way, so
Phase 1 should be scoped honestly as a myopia-focused screening test, with a note in the report that a

Phase 1 should be scoped honestly as a myopia-focused screening test, with a note in the report that a
separate near-point/accommodation-based test would be required to screen for hyperopia.
8. Phase 2 — Smartphone Eccentric Photorefraction (Detailed
Working)
This is the stretch/differentiator module. It uses the phone's camera and flash together, exploiting a
well-known optical phenomenon called the red-reflex / crescent effect.
Figure 8.1 — Step-by-step processing flow for the phone-based photorefraction method.
8.1 The underlying optical principle
A phone's flash sits slightly off-center from its camera lens. When a person looks directly at the camera
while the flash fires, light bounces off the retina and returns toward the camera — but only the part of

while the flash fires, light bounces off the retina and returns toward the camera — but only the part of
the pupil that is sufficiently out of focus lets that light escape back out, creating a bright

crescent-shaped glow within the pupil in the photo. Critically:

If the crescent appears on the same side as the flash → the eye is myopic (nearsighted).

If the crescent appears on the opposite side from the flash → the eye is hyperopic (farsighted).
This alone gives a myopia-vs-hyperopia classification without any heavy computation, using basic
OpenCV image processing (pupil detection + thresholding + side-of-crescent check).
8.2 Estimating severity
For rough magnitude, the system measures the crescent's width and the pupil's diameter in the
captured image and computes their ratio:
Crescent-to-Pupil Ratio = crescent width / pupil diameter
This ratio is a standard feature used in photorefraction research and tracks refractive error reasonably

This ratio is a standard feature used in photorefraction research and tracks refractive error reasonably
well up to roughly ±4.00 D. Beyond that range the crescent shape becomes more circular and loses its
ability to distinguish magnitude — this should be documented as a known limitation, not treated as a
bug.
8.3 Calibration, not pure theory
Even professional/commercial photorefraction tools do not derive power from a clean formula — they
calibrate empirically against measured data. The project should follow the same approach: collect
crescent-ratio measurements from volunteers alongside their known prescriptions, then fit a regression
curve (e.g., using scikit-learn or SciPy) mapping ratio → estimated power, rather than trying to derive
the mapping from optics alone.

curve (e.g., using scikit-learn or SciPy) mapping ratio → estimated power, rather than trying to derive
the mapping from optics alone.
8.4 Astigmatism cue (optional extension)
No extra hardware is needed: capture one flash image with the phone held normally, and a second with
the phone rotated 90 degrees. Comparing the crescent widths between the two orientations gives a
basic signal for astigmatism, since astigmatic eyes focus differently along different meridians.
8.5 Practical build notes

Dim ambient lighting helps — dilated pupils give a larger, clearer crescent to measure.

Fix the phone on a small stand at a consistent distance rather than holding it by hand, so calibration
stays valid across sessions.



Fix the phone on a small stand at a consistent distance rather than holding it by hand, so calibration
stays valid across sessions.

Scope Phase 2 honestly as classification + severity bucket (e.g., "mild / moderate / high"), not an
exact diopter value — this is realistic for a semester timeline and still a strong, demo-worthy result.

12. Testing & Validation Plan
The strongest part of your final report will be real accuracy numbers, not just a working demo. Follow
the same validation approach used in the published research referenced in Section 4:
1
Recruit 15–20 test subjects with a known, existing glasses/contact lens prescription (classmates,
family, faculty).
2
For each subject, run Phase 1 three times and record the average estimated power.

3

4

5

and actual power.
6

most convincing figure in a final-year evaluation.
7

13. Limitations & Scope Boundaries
Stating limitations clearly and early in your report is a strength, not a weakness — it shows the

13. Limitations & Scope Boundaries
Stating limitations clearly and early in your report is a strength, not a weakness — it shows the
evaluators you understand exactly where real clinical autorefractors still outperform your system.










14. Future Enhancements


Deep learning-based photorefraction: research such as the CNN+RNN model "REDNet" predicts
full sphere, cylinder, and spherical-equivalent power directly from multiple photorefraction images —
a strong direction for future work once a larger training dataset is available.

Mobile app packaging (Android/iOS) for wider real-world deployment beyond the lab/demo setting.

Cloud-based calibration sharing so the system improves accuracy as more validated sessions are
collected across devices.

Integration with a simple telemedicine referral flow for users flagged as likely needing a real eye
exam.

Lecture 1: Overview of Vehicular Communication Systems & Evolution of Vehicular
Networks
1.1 Overview of Vehicular Communication Systems
A Vehicular Communication System (VCS) is a wireless communication system that
enables vehicles to exchange information with other vehicles, roadside infrastructure,
pedestrians, cloud servers, and communication networks. It forms the backbone of
Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) and aims to improve road safety, traffic
efficiency, and driving comfort.

Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) and aims to improve road safety, traffic
efficiency, and driving comfort.
With the rapid increase in the number of vehicles, urban areas are experiencing severe traffic
congestion, frequent accidents, longer travel times, and environmental pollution. Traditional
traffic management methods are no longer sufficient to address these issues. Vehicular
communication systems provide an intelligent solution by enabling real-time communication
among vehicles and transportation infrastructure.
Unlike conventional communication systems, vehicular communication supports high-speed
mobile nodes (vehicles), dynamic network topology, low communication latency, and rapid
information dissemination. These features allow vehicles to exchange critical information

information dissemination. These features allow vehicles to exchange critical information
such as speed, location, direction, braking status, and road conditions in real time.
The system uses various wireless communication technologies such as Dedicated Short-
Range Communication (DSRC), Cellular Vehicle-to-Everything (C-V2X), Wi-Fi, LTE,
and 5G to establish reliable communication links.
1.2 Need for Vehicular Communication Systems
The increasing demand for safe and efficient transportation has created the need for
intelligent communication among vehicles.
The major reasons for adopting vehicular communication systems include:
 Increasing number of road accidents
 Heavy traffic congestion in urban areas
 High fuel consumption due to traffic delays

 Increasing number of road accidents
 Heavy traffic congestion in urban areas
 High fuel consumption due to traffic delays
 Environmental pollution caused by traffic jams
 Need for emergency response systems
 Requirement for autonomous and connected vehicles
 Smart city transportation management
By enabling continuous communication, vehicles can anticipate potential hazards, receive
real-time traffic updates, and make informed driving decisions.

1.3 Objectives of Vehicular Communication Systems
The primary objectives of vehicular communication systems are:
 Improve road safety by reducing accidents.
 Enable real-time communication among vehicles.
 Reduce traffic congestion through intelligent traffic management.
 Minimize travel time using dynamic route guidance.
 Support autonomous and connected vehicles.
 Improve fuel efficiency and reduce emissions.
 Provide infotainment and Internet services to passengers.
 Enhance emergency response and disaster management.
 Integrate transportation systems with smart city infrastructure.
1.4 Components of Vehicular Communication Systems
A vehicular communication system consists of several interconnected components.
1. Vehicle (On-Board Unit – OBU)

A vehicular communication system consists of several interconnected components.
1. Vehicle (On-Board Unit – OBU)
Every connected vehicle is equipped with an On-Board Unit (OBU), which acts as the
communication device. The OBU collects data from vehicle sensors and exchanges
information with nearby vehicles and roadside infrastructure.
Functions of the OBU include:
 Wireless communication
 GPS positioning
 Processing safety messages
 Navigation support
 Internet connectivity
2. Roadside Unit (RSU)
Roadside Units are communication devices installed along roads, highways, and
intersections. They communicate with passing vehicles and act as gateways to the traffic
management center.
Functions include:
 Broadcasting traffic information
 Receiving vehicle status information

management center.
Functions include:
 Broadcasting traffic information
 Receiving vehicle status information
 Traffic signal coordination
 Electronic toll collection
 Emergency notification
3. Traffic Management Center (TMC)
The Traffic Management Center receives information from multiple roadside units and
monitors traffic conditions over a large geographical area.

Functions include:
 Traffic monitoring
 Congestion control
 Accident management
 Route optimization
 Emergency coordination
4. Cloud Server
Cloud computing provides centralized storage and processing for vehicular data.
Functions include:
 Big data storage
 Navigation services
 Software updates
 Artificial Intelligence applications
 Fleet management
5. GPS Satellites
Global Positioning System (GPS) satellites provide accurate vehicle location and time
synchronization.
Functions include:
 Vehicle localization
 Route planning
 Speed estimation
 Navigation assistance
1.5 Working of Vehicular Communication Systems
The operation of a vehicular communication system can be explained as follows:
1. Vehicle sensors continuously monitor parameters such as speed, location, direction,

1. Vehicle sensors continuously monitor parameters such as speed, location, direction,
braking status, and engine condition.
2. The On-Board Unit processes the collected information.
3. The information is transmitted wirelessly to nearby vehicles or roadside
infrastructure.
4. Roadside Units forward important information to the Traffic Management Center
through communication networks.
5. The Traffic Management Center analyzes the information and sends traffic alerts,
accident warnings, and navigation guidance to vehicles.
6. Vehicles receive these messages and assist the driver or autonomous driving system in
making safe decisions.
This continuous exchange of information enables real-time traffic management and accident
prevention.

Vehicular communication systems support numerous applications in transportation.

Safety is the most important application of vehicular communication.
Examples include:

 Wrong-way driving alerts
 Road hazard notification
 Emergency vehicle priority
These applications significantly reduce road accidents and improve driver awareness.

The development of vehicular communication has evolved over several decades.

1.9 Limitations of Vehicular Communication Systems
Despite their benefits, vehicular communication systems face several challenges:
 High deployment cost.
 Frequent network topology changes.

5.1 Introduction
Cellular Vehicle-to-Everything (C-V2X) is an advanced wireless communication
technology developed by the 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) to support
Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS). It enables vehicles to communicate with other
vehicles, roadside infrastructure, pedestrians, cloud servers, and mobile networks using 4G
LTE and 5G cellular technologies.
As the number of connected and autonomous vehicles increases, there is a growing demand
for reliable, low-latency, and high-speed communication. C-V2X addresses these
requirements by providing both direct communication between nearby vehicles and
network-based communication through cellular infrastructure.

requirements by providing both direct communication between nearby vehicles and
network-based communication through cellular infrastructure.
Unlike DSRC, which mainly supports short-range communication, C-V2X offers wider
coverage, better scalability, and seamless Internet connectivity. It is considered one of the key

5.2 Definition

establish communication links while moving.

accidents. VANETs were introduced to improve road safety, enhance traffic efficiency, and

6.5 Working Principle of VANET
The operation of VANET involves continuous communication among vehicles and roadside
infrastructure.
Initially, vehicle sensors collect information such as speed, location, direction, acceleration,
braking status, and engine condition.
The collected information is processed by the On-Board Unit (OBU), which broadcasts safety
messages through wireless communication.
Nearby vehicles receive these messages and analyze the information to determine whether
there is any possibility of collision or traffic hazard.
Roadside Units also receive the information and forward it to the Traffic Management
Center.
The Traffic Management Center analyzes traffic conditions and sends traffic alerts, route
guidance, and emergency warnings back to vehicles.

6.11 VANET Compared with MANET
Although VANET is derived from Mobile Ad-hoc Networks (MANETs), there are significant
differences.
MANET supports communication among general mobile devices such as smartphones and
laptops, whereas VANET specifically supports communication among vehicles.
Vehicles move at much higher speeds than mobile devices, resulting in rapid topology
changes and shorter communication durations.
Unlike MANET, VANET heavily depends on GPS, Roadside Units, and Intelligent
Transportation Systems.
